title: Charles Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 was first built in 1991, and it works

cover.alt: The Science Museum's Difference Engine No. 2 in a glass case: a long frame of bronze and steel columns of number wheels.

body: Charles Babbage wanted a machine to calculate mathematical tables without human slips. The British government funded his first engine from 1823 but gave up in 1842, after paying over £17,000, with no working engine: the metalworking of the day couldn't economically make precise parts in the numbers needed. Babbage then drew up an improved **Difference Engine No. 2** between 1846 and 1849, but never built it. In 1985–1991 London's Science Museum did, from his drawings and to tolerances 19th-century workshops could have managed. It worked, settling a long debate over whether his design could ever have run.

slides.question: How many parts are in the Difference Engine No. 2 that London's Science Museum built?
slides.explanation: About 8,000 parts, weighing about 5 tons. It holds eight numbers of 31 decimal digits each.

slides.heading: Babbage's second design was much leaner
slides.note: No. 1 was planned at about 25,000 parts and 4 tons; No. 2 borrowed ideas from his Analytical Engine.

slides.alt: Close-up of stacked brass number wheels engraved with digits 0 to 9, with toothed sector gears between the columns.
slides.caption: Each column is a stack of number wheels. When a wheel passes from 9 to 0, a small tab trips a lever that carries 1 to the next digit.

events.text: Babbage announces a small working engine

slides.heading: Why it needed a printer
slides.text: Babbage realised that many errors in printed tables came not from bad arithmetic but from slips when setting the type. So his engine was meant to press its results into soft plaster, making moulds for printing plates with no human copying in between.

slides.heading: Small fixes, big answer
slides.text: Turning Babbage's drawings into plans a modern workshop could follow revealed a few minor errors, which the builders corrected. The finished machine is cranked by hand through a 4:1 gear: four turns of the handle for each full cycle.

slides.question: Why did the Science Museum aim to finish the engine in 1991?
slides.explanation: The build was timed to celebrate the 200th anniversary of Babbage's birth, in 1791.
